rules.point: réamhfhocail le briathra, riail ghinearálta
rules.text: Certain verbs are always followed by a particular simple preposition, and the pupil must learn which preposition goes with which verb.

rules.point: forainmneacha réamhfhoclacha
rules.text: When one of these prepositions is followed by a personal pronoun (mé, tú, é, í, sinn, sibh, iad), the two fuse into a single prepositional pronoun, for example ar + mé becomes orm. Each preposition has its own table of seven forms, given as a Dul siar (revision) box. The forms are the same in Ulster usage.

rules.point: briathra + ar
rules.text: Verbs that take ar include cuir (ar: put on, of clothing), beir (ar: catch), amharc and teip (ar: fail, the person failing is the object of ar). Further examples: cnag ar, scairt ar, tosaigh ar, iarr ar (the person asked), crom ar, cuimhnigh ar, cuir isteach ar. After ar and the singular article, Ulster lenites: ar an bhord, ar an fhón.

rules.point: briathra + de
rules.text: Verbs that take de include fiafraigh de (ask a question of someone), bain de (take off, of clothing), tit de (fall off) and tóg de (lift off). Further examples: lean de (continue with) and stad de (stop). Before the article de becomes den, which lenites: den bhean, den dréimire, den urlár.

rules.point: briathra + le
rules.text: Verbs that take le include éist le (listen to), cabhraigh le (help; Ulster also says cuidigh le), buail le (meet) and díol le (sell to). Further examples: éirigh le (succeed), tig le (be able; the Ulster form), taitin le (please, be enjoyed by) and abair le (tell someone). After le and the singular article, Ulster lenites rather than eclipses: leis an bhean, leis an mhúinteoir. Before s the article gives t: leis an tseanbhean.

rules.point: briathra + do
rules.text: Verbs that take do include tabhair do (give to), inis do (tell to) and taispeáin do (show to). Further examples: geall do (promise), lig do (allow), mol do (advise), tar do (suit, of clothes; Ulster also says fóir do) and beannaigh do (greet). Before the article do becomes don, which lenites: don chailín, don ghirseach.

rules.point: briathra + chuig
rules.text: Verbs that take chuig (towards, to a person) include scríobh chuig (write to) and caith chuig (throw to). After chuig and the singular article, Ulster lenites: chuig an mhadadh, chuig an phríomhoide.

rules.point: briathra + ó
rules.text: Verbs that take ó (from) include faigh ó (get from) and teastaigh ó (be needed or wanted by; the person wanting is the object of ó). Ó lenites a following noun: ó Mháire, ó Sheán. Before the article ó becomes ón, which lenites: ón bhaile, ón scoil.

rules.point: briathra + as
rules.text: Verbs that take as include íoc as (pay for), díol as (also pay for: díol means both sell and pay, and in Donegal Irish díol is the ordinary verb for pay, so dhíol mé as means I paid for it) and éirigh as (give up). After as and the singular article, Ulster lenites: as an bhaile, as an charr.

rules.point: an aidiacht: na dóigheanna lena húsáid
rules.text: An adjective can be used in three ways: after the verb tá as a predicate (Tá sé tuirseach), in a copula exclamation of the shape Is + adjective + an + noun + é (Is deas an rothar é), or directly after the noun it describes (bean bhocht, asal beag dubh).

rules.point: an aidiacht i ndiaidh ainmfhocail bhaininscnigh: séimhiú
rules.text: When the adjective follows a feminine singular noun it is lenited (bean bhocht, girseach bheag); after a masculine noun it is not (asal beag dubh, gasúr beag). This also holds after a preposition and the article, where Ulster lenites the noun as well: ar an bhean chráifeach.

rules.point: céimeanna comparáide: breischéim agus sárchéim
rules.text: The comparative is formed with níos plus the comparative form of the adjective (Tá Séamas níos airde) and the superlative with is plus the same form (Is é Tomás an duine is airde). The comparative form is the same in both degrees.

rules.point: breischéim: aidiachtaí a chríochnaíonn ar chonsan leathan
rules.text: For a plain adjective ending in a broad consonant, slenderise the final consonant and add -e: ard becomes airde. Other examples given: bán, bocht, bog, caol, dearg, fuar, glas (báine, boichte, boige, caoile, deirge, fuaire, glaise).

rules.point: breischéim: aidiachtaí ar -ach agus -each
rules.text: An adjective ending in -ach changes -ach to -aí, and one ending in -each changes -each to -í: feargach becomes feargaí, díreach becomes dírí.

rules.point: breischéim: aidiachtaí ar -úil
rules.text: An adjective ending in -úil adds -a: éirimiúil becomes éirimiúla, cairdiúil becomes cairdiúla.

rules.point: breischéim: aidiachtaí ar -mhar agus -ar
rules.text: An adjective ending in -mhar (or -ar) adds -e with slenderisation: luachmhar becomes luachmhaire, lúfar becomes lúfaire.

rules.point: breischéim: aidiachtaí a gcailltear guta iontu (coimriú)
rules.text: Some two-syllable adjectives drop the vowel of the last syllable and add -e: ramhar becomes raimhre. The same type: folamh, daingean, íseal, uasal, álainn, domhain, saibhir, deacair, aoibhinn (foilmhe, daingne, ísle, uaisle, áille, doimhne, saibhre, deacra, aoibhne). Ulster usage is the same as the standard here.

rules.point: comparáid chothrom: chomh ... le
rules.text: To say as ... as, use chomh with the basic form of the adjective, not the comparative form, followed by le (Níl Muiris chomh fiosrach le Liam) or by is a (Níl sé chomh ceomhar anocht is a bhí sé aréir). Note that le followed by the article lenites in Ulster: chomh ceanúil leis an mhadadh.

rules.point: breischéim: níos ... ná, i bhfad níos
rules.text: The thing compared is introduced with ná (Tá an áit seo níos contúirtí ná an áit eile), and i bhfad before níos strengthens the comparison (Tá ola i bhfad níos flúirsí anois).

rules.point: aidiachtaí a bhfuil breischéim ar leith acu
rules.text: A small group of common adjectives has an irregular comparative form that must be learnt: maith, níos fearr; olc, níos measa; mór, níos mó; beag, níos lú; fada, níos faide; furast, níos fusa; te, níos teo; tréan, níos treise or níos tréine; breá, níos breátha. The same form follows is in the superlative.

lessons.rule: After tá (or bhí, bíonn), write the adjective in its plain form with no change: Tá Ciara díograiseach.

lessons.title: Chomh ... le
lessons.rule: To say as ... as, use chomh + the plain adjective + le: chomh fiosrach le Liam. Put h before an adjective beginning with a vowel (chomh hard), and write leis an before a noun with the article (leis an mhadadh).
steps: Find chomh: it takes the plain adjective, never the níos form.
Keep ard as it is, but add h because it begins with a vowel: hard.
Add le before the other person: Tá Ciara chomh hard lena deartháir.

rules.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, iolraí laga: caolú
rules.text: Most weak plurals in the first declension are formed simply by making the final consonant of the word slender, for example bád becomes báid.

rules.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, iolraí laga: -a a chur leis
rules.text: Some first-declension plurals are formed by adding -a to the word, for example ceart becomes cearta.

rules.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, tréaniolraí
rules.text: Some words in this group have strong plurals, for example dán becomes dánta and cogadh becomes cogaí.

rules.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, inscne
rules.text: All first-declension nouns are masculine.

rules.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, deireadh an fhocail
rules.text: First-declension nouns end in a broad consonant.

rules.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, an tuiseal ginideach uatha
rules.text: The nominative singular is made slender to form the genitive singular, and the noun is lenited after the article where possible, for example an capall gives cosa an chapaill. This is the same in Ulster: the genitive singular after an lenites b, c, f, g, m and p, and leaves d and t alone (adharca an tairbh, dath an dorais).

rules.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, an tuiseal ginideach iolra
rules.text: The genitive plural has the same form as the nominative singular, and after na it is eclipsed where possible, for example seolta na mbád, cosa na gcapall. Ulster does not differ here: eclipsis after na in the genitive plural is standard everywhere.

rules.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, focail a thosaíonn ar ghuta
rules.text: Nouns beginning with a vowel take t- in the nominative singular (an t-úll), nothing in the genitive singular (dath an úill), h in the nominative plural (na húlla, na hoileáin) and n- in the genitive plural (dath na n-úll, muintir na n-oileán).

rules.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, focail a thosaíonn ar s + guta
rules.text: Nouns beginning with s followed by a vowel take t before the s in the genitive singular after the article (cóta an tsagairt, doras an tséipéil) but are unchanged in the genitive plural (cótaí na sagart, doirse na séipéal).

rules.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, focail a chríochnaíonn ar -ach, -each
rules.text: Nouns ending in -ach or -each change that ending to -aigh or -igh in the genitive singular and the nominative plural (an marcach, cáipín an mharcaigh, na marcaigh), while the genitive plural keeps the -ach form with eclipsis (cáipíní na marcach, oifigí na gcléireach).

rules.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, athraíonn ea go i
rules.text: When the noun has ea before the final consonant, ea changes to i in the genitive singular and the nominative plural, for example an fear, teach an fhir, na fir, tithe na bhfear.

rules.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, athraíonn éa go éi
rules.text: When the noun has éa before the final consonant, éa changes to éi in the genitive singular and the nominative plural, for example an páipéar, dath an pháipéir, na páipéir, dath na bpáipéar.

rules.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, athraíonn íoch go igh
rules.text: Nouns ending in -íoch change that ending to -igh in the genitive singular and the nominative plural, for example an beithíoch, luach an bheithígh, na beithígh, luach na mbeithíoch. Beithíoch is a common Ulster word for an animal or beast (in Donegal often a horse), so pupils will meet it often.

rules.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, athraíonn ia go éi
rules.text: When the noun has ia before the final consonant, ia changes to éi in the genitive singular and the nominative plural, for example an t-iasc, praghas an éisc, na héisc, praghas na n-iasc.

lessons.en: Weak plural: make the last consonant slender
lessons.rule: For other first-declension nouns, put i after the last vowel so the final consonant is slender: crann becomes crainn, gasúr becomes gasúir. Where the last vowel is ea it changes to i (peann, pinn), and éa changes to éi (ticéad, ticéid).
steps: Find the last vowel in crann: a.
Put i after it so the nn becomes slender: crainn.
Write it after na: Tá na crainn ag cailleadh a gcuid duilleog san fhómhar.

rules.point: an dara díochlaonadh, an uimhir iolra: -í
rules.text: The plural of a second declension noun can be formed by adding -í to the word, as in oifig, oifigí.

rules.point: an dara díochlaonadh, an uimhir iolra: -anna, -eanna
rules.text: The plural can be formed by adding -anna or -eanna to the word, as in scoil, scoileanna and ceist, ceisteanna.

rules.point: an dara díochlaonadh, an uimhir iolra: -a
rules.text: The plural can be formed by adding -a to the word, as in amharclann, amharclanna.

rules.point: an dara díochlaonadh, an uimhir iolra: -acha
rules.text: The plural can be formed by adding -acha to the word, as in craobh, craobhacha.

rules.point: an dara díochlaonadh, tréithe ginearálta
rules.text: Most of the nouns in this group are feminine, and they end in a consonant.

rules.point: an dara díochlaonadh, tuiseal ginideach uatha: an t-alt
rules.text: In the genitive singular the article an changes to na, and the noun is not lenited after it: an fháinleog becomes sciathán na fáinleoige. This is the same in Ulster.

rules.point: an dara díochlaonadh, tuiseal ginideach uatha: -e
rules.text: The commonest way of forming the genitive singular is to add -e to the noun, as in an scoil, doras na scoile.

rules.point: an dara díochlaonadh, tuiseal ginideach uatha: -each go -í
rules.text: A noun ending in -each changes that ending to -í in the genitive singular, as in an ghirseach, cóta na girsí. Girseach is the everyday Ulster word for a girl, so this example suits the school well.

rules.point: an dara díochlaonadh, tuiseal ginideach uatha: caolú agus -e
rules.text: A noun ending in a broad consonant is slenderised and takes -e in the genitive singular, as in an phictiúrlann, clár na pictiúrlainne.

rules.point: an dara díochlaonadh, tuiseal ginideach: focail a thosaíonn ar ghuta
rules.text: A noun beginning with a vowel takes h after na in the genitive singular and n- after na in the genitive plural: an oifig, doras na hoifige, doirse na n-oifigí.

rules.point: an dara díochlaonadh, rialacha caolaithe
rules.text: When the noun is slenderised for the genitive singular, ea becomes i in words of more than one syllable (doineann, doininne), ea becomes ei in others (speach, speiche), with cearc, circe as an exception, and ia becomes éi (grian, gréine).

rules.point: an dara díochlaonadh, tuiseal ginideach iolra
rules.text: In the genitive plural the article na eclipses a following consonant and puts n- before a vowel, and nouns whose plural ends in -a lose that ending (na bróga, dath na mbróg) while nouns whose plural ends in -anna, -eanna or -í keep it (na fadhbanna, tús na bhfadhbanna). Eclipsis after na in the genitive plural applies in Ulster exactly as in the standard; the Ulster lenition after a preposition and the article (ar an bhord) does not affect this.

rules.point: an tuiseal ginideach i ndiaidh an ainm bhriathartha
rules.text: A noun that is the object of a verbal noun goes into the genitive case, as in ag canadh amhráin, ag cur báistí (or, in Ulster, ag cur fearthainne), ag glanadh na fuinneoige. This is stated on page 141 for first declension nouns and repeated on page 149 for second declension nouns.

tables.title: An Dara Díochlaonadh: Iolraí (cumtar an uimhir iolra)
forms: (i) Trí -í a chur leis an fhocal: Oifig, Oifigí
(ii) Trí -anna, -eanna a chur leis an fhocal: Scoil, Scoileanna; Ceist, Ceisteanna
(iii) Trí -a a chur leis an fhocal: Amharclann, Amharclanna
(iv) Trí -acha a chur leis an fhocal: Craobh, Craobhacha

tables.title: Iolraí: samplaí (uatha agus iolra)
An Dara Díochlaonadh: samplaí, uatha agus iolra, ainmneach agus ginideach
forms: 1 (-e): An scoil, na scoileanna; Doras na scoile, Doirse na scoileanna
2 (each > í): An ghirseach, na girseacha; Cóta na girsí, cótaí na ngirseach
3 (caolú + e): An phictiúrlann, na pictiúrlanna; Clár na pictiúrlainne, cláracha na bpictiúrlann
4 (-e) Focail a thosaíonn ar ghuta: An oifig, na hoifigí; Doras na hoifige, doirse na n-oifigí

tables.title: Déantar caolú de réir na rialacha seo
forms: ea > ei: speach, speiche. Ach: cearc, circe

lessons.title: An chéad díochlaonadh: an ginideach uatha
lessons.en: First declension: genitive singular with an
lessons.rule: When a noun follows another noun such as barr, doras or lár, it goes into the genitive: after an, put séimhiú on it and make its last consonant slender, so an crann becomes barr an chrainn.
steps: Put séimhiú on the first letter: crann becomes chrann.
Make the last consonant slender by putting i after the last vowel: chrainn.
Write it after an: Thit an cat ó bharr an chrainn.

example.prompt: Thit an cat ó bharr an (crann).
example.answer: Thit an cat ó bharr an chrainn.

more.answer: Chuaigh muid go deireadh an bhóthair.
Bhí inneall an bháid briste.

lessons.hint: After an: séimhiú at the start, i before the last consonant.

lessons.title: An chéad díochlaonadh: s, d, t agus guta
lessons.en: First declension: nouns beginning with s, d, t or a vowel
lessons.rule: Make the end slender as usual, but watch the first letter: after an, s followed by a vowel becomes ts (an tsagairt), while d, t, sc and vowels do not change (an tuaiscirt, an scéil, an asail).
steps: Make the last consonant slender: sagart becomes sagairt.
It begins with s and a vowel, so put t in front of it after an: an tsagairt.

lessons.en: First declension: genitive without the article
lessons.rule: With no an in front, do not add séimhiú: just make the last consonant slender, so arán becomes píosa aráin. A boy's or man's name is the exception: it takes séimhiú too (Cathal, camán Chathail).

lessons.rule: A noun that comes after a verbal noun such as ag glanadh or ag léamh goes into the genitive, just as it would after another noun: ag glanadh an chlóis, ag léamh na ceiste, ag léamh na gceisteanna.
steps: The noun follows ag glanadh, so it goes into the genitive.
Clós is masculine: put séimhiú on it after an and make the end slender, an chlóis.
Write the phrase: ag glanadh an chlóis.

example.answer: ag glanadh an chlóis

lessons.hint: After ag + verbal noun, use the genitive.

rules.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, an uimhir iolra: -anna
rules.text: Some third-declension nouns form their plural by adding -anna to the word: rang becomes ranganna.

rules.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, an uimhir iolra: -í
rules.text: Most third-declension nouns, including the agent nouns in -éir, -eoir, -óir, -úir and abstract nouns in -acht and -int, form their plural by adding -í: cainteoir becomes cainteoirí, beannacht becomes beannachtaí, canúint becomes canúintí.

rules.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, an uimhir iolra: -acha
rules.text: Some third-declension nouns form their plural by adding -acha to the word: barúil becomes barúlacha.

rules.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, an uimhir iolra: -ta, -te
rules.text: Some third-declension nouns form their plural by adding -ta or -te to the word: gleann becomes gleannta.

rules.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, inscne
rules.text: The third declension contains both masculine and feminine nouns.

rules.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, deireadh an fhocail
rules.text: Every noun in the third declension ends in a consonant.

rules.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, an tuiseal ginideach uatha: -a
rules.text: The genitive singular is formed by adding -a to the word. If the final consonant is slender it is made broad first: éir becomes éara, eoir becomes eora, óir becomes óra, úir becomes úra.

rules.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, an tuiseal ginideach uatha: io go ea
rules.text: In one-syllable words the vowel group io changes to ea in the genitive: sioc gives seaca (ag cur seaca), fios gives feasa (ag lorg feasa).

rules.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, an tuiseal ginideach uatha: focail ar -int
rules.text: In words ending in -int the t is dropped after broadening in the genitive: tuiscint becomes tuisceana.

rules.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, an tuiseal ginideach uatha: focail ar -irt
rules.text: In words ending in -irt the t becomes tha after broadening in the genitive: buairt becomes buartha.

rules.point: an tuiseal ginideach i ndiaidh an ainm bhriathartha
rules.text: The genitive case follows a verbal noun: ag ól fíona, ag foghlaim an cheachta.

lessons.title: Iolra -í: -óir, -eoir, -éir
lessons.rule: Nouns for people ending in -óir, -eoir or -éir add -í in the plural: múinteoir becomes múinteoirí.
steps: Múinteoir ends in -eoir, so it takes -í.
Add -í: múinteoirí.
Write it after na: Beidh na múinteoirí ag obair go déanach sa scoil anocht.

lessons.rule: For a noun ending in -óir, -eoir, -éir or -úir, take out the i and add -a (-óra, -eora, -éara, -úra); after an, add séimhiú as well, but leave d, t and s alone.

lessons.rule: A noun after a verbal noun such as ag moladh or ag scríobh goes into the genitive: an ceoltóir becomes ag moladh an cheoltóra, an nuacht becomes ag scríobh na nuachta.
steps: The noun follows ag moladh, so it goes into the genitive.

Put séimhiú on it after an: Ag moladh an cheoltóra.

rules.point: an ceathrú díochlaonadh, tréaniolraí
rules.text: Nouns of the fourth declension have strong plurals, and most of them end in -í, -te, -the or -anna in the plural.

rules.point: an ceathrú díochlaonadh, iolra -í
rules.text: Nouns ending in -ín in the singular, and most nouns ending in -a, -e or -aire, add í to form the plural (an siopa, na siopaí; an béile, na béilí; an cócaire, na cócairí).

rules.point: an ceathrú díochlaonadh, iolra -te/-the
rules.text: Nouns ending in -aí or -í, and a small group ending in -é or -e, add -te or -the in the plural (an t-ainmhí, na hainmhithe; an scéalaí, na scéalaithe; an ghné, na gnéithe; an líne, na línte; an tine, na tinte).

rules.point: an ceathrú díochlaonadh, iolra -anna
rules.text: Nouns ending in -o or -u, and some nouns ending in -a or -á, add -anna in the plural (an cú, na cúnna; an cnó, na cnónna; an trá, na tránna; an tua, na tuanna).

rules.point: an ceathrú díochlaonadh, iolra -anna (focail eile)
rules.text: A further group of nouns in this declension, mostly short loan words and words ending in -é, also take -anna in the plural (an bus, na busanna; an ghé, na géanna).

rules.point: an ceathrú díochlaonadh, iolraí neamhrialta
rules.text: Some fourth-declension nouns follow none of the patterns A to D and their plurals must be learned individually (an gabha, na gaibhne; an contae, na contaethe; an comhrá, na comhráite; an t-ainm, na hainmneacha; an oíche, na hoícheanta).

rules.point: an ceathrú díochlaonadh, críoch na bhfocal
rules.text: In the fourth declension almost every noun ends in -ín or in a vowel.

rules.point: an ceathrú díochlaonadh, inscne
rules.text: Most fourth-declension nouns are masculine, but there are feminine nouns in it too.

rules.point: an ceathrú díochlaonadh, tuiseal ginideach uatha, firinscneach
rules.text: In the genitive singular the noun itself does not change; after the article an, a masculine noun is lenited (teach an chailín, dath an bhosca) and t is normally prefixed to a noun beginning with s (fear an tsiopa). A vowel-initial noun takes no prefix (praghas an oráiste).

rules.point: an ceathrú díochlaonadh, tuiseal ginideach uatha, baininscneach
rules.text: In the genitive singular of a feminine noun the article changes from an to na, and h is prefixed to a noun beginning with a vowel (tús na haiste, éide na banaltra, barr na sleá).

rules.point: an ceathrú díochlaonadh, tuiseal ginideach iolra
rules.text: The genitive plural has the same form as the nominative plural, with na before it; the noun is eclipsed after na (tithe na gcailíní, dath na mboscaí, éidí na mbanaltraí) and n- is prefixed to a vowel (praghas na n-oráistí, tús na n-aistí).

rules.point: an tuiseal ginideach i ndiaidh an ainm bhriathartha
rules.text: A noun that follows a verbal noun (ag oscailt, ag scríobh) goes into the genitive: ag oscailt an fhéirín, ag scríobh na haiste. This is the same in Ulster; note that ag amharc ar (Ulster for ag féachaint ar) takes ar and so does not put the noun in the genitive.

tables.title: Iolra -í: focail a chríochnaíonn ar -(a)ire
Iolra -te/-the: samplaí (Ainmneach Uatha, Ainmneach Iolra)
Iolra -te/-the: focail a chríochnaíonn ar -aí, ar -í, agus roinnt focal ar -é agus -e
forms: (-aí) Gréasaí, ceannaí, ceardaí, cleasaí, Críostaí, gadaí, moncaí
(-í) Ní, oibrí, dlí, rí, croí, slí
(-é, -e) Gné, líne, tine, tuile, féile (na gnéithe, na línte, na tinte, na tuilte, na féilte)

tables.title: Iolra -anna: samplaí (Ainmneach Uatha, Ainmneach Iolra)
Iolra -anna: focail a chríochnaíonn ar -o, -u, -a, -á
forms: Lao, ceo, brú, liú, tlú, bia, fia, nia, bua, bá, fleá, grua, íomhá, sleá, glao, rogha.

tables.title: Iolra -anna: focail eile (Ainmneach Uatha, Ainmneach Iolra)
Iolra -anna: focail eile
forms: Ceant, pas, seans, seic, snáithe, sraoth, stop, téacs, cé, cré, ré.

lessons.title: Iolra -í
lessons.rule: For a fourth-declension noun ending in -a or -ín, add -í in the plural (mála, málaí; sicín, sicíní); for one ending in -e, change the -e to -í (ceapaire, ceapairí).
steps: Mála ends in -a, so add -í.
The plural is málaí.
Write it after na: Fág na málaí ag an doras, le do thoil.

example.answer: Fág na málaí ag an doras, le do thoil.

lessons.hint: Add -í; a final -e becomes -í.

rules.point: an cúigiú díochlaonadh, inscne
rules.text: Most nouns in the fifth declension are feminine.

rules.point: an cúigiú díochlaonadh, deireadh an ainmnigh uatha
rules.text: Fifth-declension nouns end in -in, -il, -ir or in a vowel in the nominative singular (traein, abhainn, riail, triail, cathaoir, litir, uimhir, lacha, cara, comharsa).

rules.point: an cúigiú díochlaonadh, deireadh an ghinidigh uatha
rules.text: In the genitive singular these nouns end in -ch, -n, -d or -r, which gives four main groups of nouns; Nollaig (genitive Nollag) is treated separately as a fifth group.

rules.point: an cúigiú díochlaonadh, an uimhir iolra
rules.text: Most fifth-declension nouns form their plural in -(e)acha (traenacha, litreacha, cathaoireacha, mainistreacha, aithreacha); a small number are irregular and must be learned: bráithre, caoirigh, ingne, lachain, cairde, monarchana, comharsana, naimhde, nollaigí, tríochaidí.

rules.point: an ginideach uatha ar -(e)ach
rules.text: Group A nouns add -(e)ach in the genitive singular: an chathaoir becomes na cathaoireach, an litir becomes na litreach, an eochair becomes na heochrach. Some drop a vowel (syncopate) before the ending: an chathair becomes na cathrach, an mhainistir becomes na mainistreach.

rules.point: an ginideach uatha ar -n
rules.text: Group B nouns end in -n in the genitive singular: an abhainn becomes na habhann, an chomharsa becomes na comharsan, an teorainn becomes na teorann, an mhonarcha becomes na monarchan, an ionga becomes na hiongan, an lacha becomes na lachan.

rules.point: an ginideach uatha ar -d
rules.text: Group C: cara ends in -d in the genitive singular, an cara becomes an charad (teach an charad).

rules.point: an ginideach uatha ar -r
rules.text: Group D, the family words, end in -r in the genitive singular and drop the i of the last syllable: an t-athair becomes an athar, an deartháir becomes an dearthár, an bráthair becomes an bhráthar, an mháthair becomes na máthar, and an deirfiúr becomes na deirféar.

rules.point: an ginideach uatha, Nollaig
rules.text: Group E: Nollaig has the genitive singular Nollag, tús na Nollag.

rules.point: an ginideach iolra
rules.text: For nouns whose plural ends in -(e)acha or -e the genitive plural is the same as the nominative plural, with eclipsis after na (dath na gcathaoireacha, troime na n-eochracha, tithe na gcairde); but caoirigh, comharsana and lachain take the short genitive plural caorach, comharsan, lachan (cosa na gcaorach, gairdíní na gcomharsan, cleití na lachan).

rules.point: an ginideach i ndiaidh an ainm bhriathartha
rules.text: A noun that follows a verbal noun goes into the genitive: ag casadh na heochrach, ag glanadh na monarchan.

lessons.rule: Most fifth-declension nouns add -acha or -eacha in the plural, and the vowel before the last consonant often drops out: traein, traenacha; litir, litreacha; eochair, eochracha.
steps: Drop the i before the last consonant: litir becomes litr.

rules.point: réamhfhocail chomhshuite agus an tuiseal ginideach
rules.text: A compound preposition (a simple preposition plus a noun, such as ar son, i measc, os comhair) is followed by the genitive case: the noun after it goes into the genitive, and the article becomes an (masculine), na (feminine) or na (plural) with the usual genitive mutations. Ulster usage is the same as the standard here: the lenition that Ulster uses after a simple preposition and the article (ar an bhord) does not apply after a compound preposition, because the noun is in the genitive (ar son an bhoird, ar son na tíre).

rules.point: na réamhfhocail chomhshuite is coitianta
rules.text: Each of these takes the genitive. All of them are used in Ulster; pupils will also hear fá choinne (for, to get) beside le haghaidh, and it takes the genitive in the same way.

lessons.title: Firinscneach uatha: an + séimhiú
lessons.en: Masculine nouns: keep an and lenite
lessons.rule: After a compound preposition (i gcoinne, i ndiaidh, ar chúl) the noun goes into the genitive: for a masculine noun keep an and lenite b, c, f, g, m or p (an cat: i ndiaidh an chait), then give it its genitive ending.
steps: i gcoinne is a compound preposition, so the noun goes into the genitive.
geata is masculine: keep an and lenite g: an gheata.
geata keeps the same ending: Tá an rothar ina sheasamh i gcoinne an gheata.

lessons.en: Masculine nouns beginning with d, t, l, n, r, s or a vowel
lessons.rule: A masculine noun beginning with d, t, l, n or r takes no séimhiú after an (i gcoinne an rialtais); s before a vowel or l, n, r takes t (an tseó), and a vowel loses its t- (an tAifreann: an Aifrinn). Then give the noun its genitive ending.
steps: in aice takes the genitive, and droichead is masculine, so keep an.
droichead begins with d, so do not lenite it.

lessons.title: Baininscneach uatha: na, gan séimhiú
lessons.en: Feminine nouns: an becomes na, lenition goes
lessons.rule: For a feminine noun, change an to na and take away the séimhiú or the t that an gave it (an fhoireann: na foirne; an tseachtain: na seachtaine), then give it its genitive ending.

comhra.title: Mo cheantar agus an timpeallacht
comhra.example: Tá mé i mo chónaí in áit bheag in aice le hIúr Cinn Trá.

rules.point: an t-ainm briathartha le 'ag' (Tá sé ag canadh)
rules.text: The verbal noun is used after 'ag' with the verb 'bí' to say what someone is doing now: Tá sé ag canadh, Tá sí ag scuabadh, Tá siad ag obair. Pages 178 to 181 teach this through photograph captions only. The question that goes with it in Ulster is 'Cad é atá ar siúl aige?' rather than 'Céard atá ar siúl aige?'.

rules.point: an t-ainm briathartha, -adh/-eadh
rules.text: Most one-syllable (first conjugation) verbs form the verbal noun by adding -adh after a broad ending and -eadh after a slender ending: dún, dúnadh; glan, glanadh; bris, briseadh; scaip, scaipeadh.

rules.point: an t-ainm briathartha, -t
rules.text: Verbs ending in a slender consonant such as -n, -l or -r add -t to form the verbal noun: bain, baint; tiomáin, tiomáint; oscail, oscailt; freagair, freagairt; imir, imirt.

rules.point: an t-ainm briathartha, -ú/-iú
rules.text: Most second conjugation verbs in -aigh or -igh drop that ending and take -ú (broad) or -iú (slender): gortaigh, gortú; ceartaigh, ceartú; cruinnigh, cruinniú; bailigh, bailiú.

rules.point: an t-ainm briathartha, -ach/-each
rules.text: A small group of -aigh/-igh verbs take -ach or -each instead of -ú/-iú: ceannaigh, ceannach; réitigh, réiteach; cuardaigh, cuardach; fuadaigh, fuadach; clúdaigh, clúdach.

rules.point: an t-ainm briathartha, leathnú an chonsain deiridh
rules.text: Some verbs form the verbal noun by broadening the final consonant, with no ending added: cuir, cur; siúil, siúl; iompair, iompar; ceangail, ceangal; freastail, freastal.

rules.point: an t-ainm briathartha, briathra neamhrialta
rules.text: The irregular verbs have their own verbal nouns which must be learned: abair, rá; beir, breith; bí, bheith; feic, feiceáil; ith, ithe; faigh, fáil; tar, teacht; téigh, dul; clois, cloisteáil; tabhair, tabhairt; déan, déanamh. In Ulster the verb 'cluin' (verbal noun cluinstin) is commonly used for 'clois', and 'tchí mé' is the present tense of 'feic', but the verbal noun stays 'feiceáil'.

rules.point: an t-ainm briathartha, slite éagsúla eile
rules.text: Other verbs form the verbal noun in various individual ways (-áil, -eacht, -amh, -ean, -int, -í, -ím, -íocht): nigh, ní; fág, fágáil; éirigh, éirí; lig, ligean; imigh, imeacht; cónaigh, cónaí; caith, caitheamh; seas, seasamh; dúisigh, dúiseacht; léigh, léamh; rothaigh, rothaíocht; tit, titim; inis, insint.

rules.point: an t-ainm briathartha gan athrú
rules.text: Some verbs do not change at all: the verbal noun is the same as the root, including most verbs in -áil (cniotáil, bácáil, sábháil, spáráil, tástáil, pacáil, iarnáil) and others such as díol, goid, fás, léim, rith, snámh, scríobh, troid, úsáid, obair, foghlaim, stad, gáire, ól, and in Ulster amharc.

rules.point: bí leis an ainm briathartha (an aimsir láithreach agus an aimsir ghnáthláithreach)
rules.text: The verb 'bí' is very often used with the verbal noun, for example Bíonn sé ag obair go crua. In Ulster the present forms are tá mé, tá tú, tá sé/sí, tá muid, tá sibh, tá siad (negative níl mé, níl muid; question an bhfuil mé, an bhfuil muid) and the habitual present forms are bím, bíonn tú, bíonn sé/sí, bíonn muid, bíonn sibh, bíonn siad (negative ní bhím, ní bhíonn muid; question an mbím, an mbíonn muid). The first person singular keeps its own ending (bím). The impersonal forms táthar, níltear, bítear, ní bhítear are as in the standard.

lessons.title: Tá sé ag ...: an t-ainm briathartha i ndiaidh ag
lessons.en: Saying what someone is doing: ag + verbal noun
lessons.rule: To say what someone is doing, use Tá + subject + ag + the verbal noun: glan becomes ag glanadh. Most one-syllable verbs add -adh or -eadh, verbs such as bain and oscail add -t (baint, oscailt), and some, such as ól, rith and foghlaim, do not change.
steps: Find the verb in brackets: scuab.
Make the verbal noun: a one-syllable broad verb adds -adh, so scuabadh.
Put it after ag and keep the rest: Tá Máire ag scuabadh na cistine.

example.prompt: Tá Máire ag (scuab) na cistine.
example.answer: Tá Máire ag scuabadh na cistine.

more.answer: Tá Daidí ag baint an fhéir.
Tá an madadh ag ól uisce.

lessons.hint: ag + verbal noun: -adh, -eadh, -t, or no change.

lessons.rule: When the object comes before the verbal noun, put a between them and add h after the first letter of the verbal noun: bricfeasta a dhéanamh.

lessons.rule: Many verbs change to make the verbal noun (ceartaigh: ceartú, ceannaigh: ceannach, faigh: fáil, cosain: cosaint), so find the verbal noun first and then add h after a.

lessons.rule: A vowel cannot take h, so a verbal noun that begins with a vowel stays as it is after a: an doras a oscailt.

lessons.title: Le agus ar + an t-ainm briathartha
lessons.en: Still to be done (le) and a state (ar)
lessons.rule: Use le + the verbal noun for something still to be done (ríomhphost le scríobh), and ar + the verbal noun for the state something is in (ar díol, ar lasadh). Neither le nor ar changes the verbal noun here.
steps: The work is still to be done, so use le.
Find the verbal noun of déan: déanamh.
Put it in the gap: Tá an obair bhaile le déanamh agam anocht.

rules.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha, a cumadh
rules.text: Ulster forms the verbal adjective exactly as the standard does.

rules.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha, an foirceann -ta
rules.text: Broad roots ending in l, n, s, ch and similar sounds take -ta: dall becomes dallta, dún becomes dúnta, múch becomes múchta.

rules.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha, an foirceann -te
rules.text: Slender roots take -te: bris becomes briste, mill becomes millte, roinn becomes roinnte. A root ending in slender -igh drops the -igh before -te: léigh becomes léite, pléigh becomes pléite, suigh becomes suite.

rules.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha, an foirceann -tha
rules.text: Broad roots ending in b, c, d, g, m, p or r take -tha: cíor becomes cíortha, crom becomes cromtha, fág becomes fágtha, scuab becomes scuabtha, leag becomes leagtha.

rules.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha, na foircinn -aithe agus -ithe
rules.text: Second-conjugation verbs ending in -aigh or -igh replace that ending with -aithe (broad) or -ithe (slender): críochnaigh becomes críochnaithe, ceannaigh becomes ceannaithe, deisigh becomes deisithe, imigh becomes imithe.

rules.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha, an foirceann -fa
rules.text: Roots ending in -bh or -mh replace that ending with -fa: scríobh becomes scríofa, treabh becomes treafa, lobh becomes lofa.

rules.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha le tá agus ag
rules.text: The verbal adjective is used with tá to describe a completed state (Tá an doras dúnta), and with ag plus a pronoun to say who has done the action (Tá an féar bainte agam). In Ulster the same pattern is used; where a noun follows ag and the article, lenite it: Tá an pháirc treafa ag an fheirmeoir.

lessons.title: Cá + urú
lessons.rule: Cá (where) eclipses the verb after it: Cá bhfuil tú? Cá dtéann tú? In the past, irregular verbs keep Cá with eclipsis (Cá ndeachaigh tú? Cá bhfaca tú é?), but raibh never changes (Cá raibh tú?). Regular verbs in the past take Cár and h: Cár fhág tú do mhála?
steps: Start with Cá.
Eclipse the verb: téann becomes dtéann, imríonn becomes n-imríonn.
In the past, a regular verb takes Cár and h: Cár fhág tú é?

lessons.title: Cá háit agus Cén áit
lessons.en: Where: Cá háit and Cén áit
lessons.rule: Cá háit and Cén áit (what place) are followed by a and eclipsis in the present and future: Cá háit a bhfuil sé? Cén áit a mbeidh tú? In the past, irregular verbs take a and eclipsis (Cá háit a ndeachaigh tú?), and regular verbs take ar and h (Cén áit ar fhan tú?).
steps: Start with Cá háit or Cén áit.
Add a and eclipse the verb: a bhfuil, a n-oibríonn.
In the past, a regular verb takes ar and h: Cén áit ar chas tú air?

lessons.title: Cad chuige agus Cén fáth

steps: Start with Cad chuige or Cén fáth.
Add a and eclipse the verb: a bhfuil, a n-imríonn.
In the past, a regular verb takes ar and h: Cad chuige ar fhág tú?

lessons.title: Cá mhéad
lessons.rule: Cá mhéad (how many) takes the noun in the singular, not the plural: Cá mhéad deartháir atá agat? Cá mhéad ábhar a dhéanann tú? After the noun, use atá for bí, or a and h for other verbs.
steps: Start with Cá mhéad.
Put the noun in the singular: deartháireacha becomes deartháir.
Add atá, or a and h on the verb: Cá mhéad deartháir atá agat?

lessons.title: Cén + ainmfhocal
lessons.rule: Cén (which, what) changes the noun like the article an: h on a feminine noun (Cén bhliain? Cén mhí?) and t- before a masculine noun beginning with a vowel (Cén t-am? Cén t-ábhar?). Other nouns do not change: Cén lá? Cén aois? Cén obair?
steps: Decide if the noun is masculine or feminine.
Feminine: add h (bliain becomes bhliain). Masculine with a vowel: add t- (am becomes t-am).
Anything else stays as it is: Cén lá?

example.answer: Cén bhliain a bhí ann?

more.answer: Cén t-ábhar is fearr leat?

lessons.hint: Cén works like an: h on feminine nouns, t- on masculine vowels.

lessons.title: Cad é mar agus Cén dóigh
lessons.rule: Cad é mar (how) is followed by atá for bí, or a and h: Cad é mar atá tú? Cad é mar a bhí an aimsir? Cén dóigh (in what way) is followed by a and eclipsis: Cén dóigh a bhfuil tú? Cén dóigh a dtéann tú ar scoil?
steps: Cad é mar: atá, or a + h on the verb.
Cén dóigh: a + eclipsis on the verb.
Both are everyday Ulster greetings: Cad é mar atá tú? Cén dóigh a bhfuil tú?

lessons.rule: After Sílim, Measaim, Deir sé, Cluinim and Tá a fhios agam, 'that' is go, and go eclipses the verb: Sílim go bhfuil sé fuar. Deir sí go n-imríonn sí peil. The verb keeps its tense.

lessons.title: Na briathra neamhrialta san aimsir chaite
lessons.rule: Irregular verbs follow their question form. Bí, téigh, feic, faigh, déan and abair (An raibh? An ndeachaigh? An ndúirt?) take go or nach with eclipsis: go ndeachaigh, go bhfaca, go bhfuair, go ndearna, go ndúirt; raibh never changes (go raibh). Tar, tabhair, beir, cluin and ith (Ar tháinig? Níor ith) take gur or nár: gur tháinig, gur thug, gur chuala, gur ith. In Ulster you will also hear gur dhúirt and nár dhúirt.
steps: Ask: does this verb take An or Ar in the past?
An: use go or nach, and eclipse (go ndeachaigh).
Ar: use gur or nár, with h (gur tháinig).

lessons.hint: An verbs (bí, téigh, feic, faigh, déan, abair): go/nach. Ar verbs (tar, tabhair, beir, cluin, ith): gur/nár.

steps: Add a after the noun.

Tá becomes atá, one word.

lessons.title: An diúltach díreach: nach agus nár
lessons.rule: For who ... not or which ... not, drop ní and use nach with eclipsis: an cailín nach n-imríonn peil, an fear nach bhfuil anseo, an bus nach mbeidh in am. In the past, a regular verb takes nár and h: an fear nár fhreagair an fón. Irregular verbs follow their question form: nár tháinig, nár ith (Ar tháinig?), but nach ndeachaigh, nach bhfuair, nach raibh (An ndeachaigh?).
steps: Drop ní or níor (níl becomes nach bhfuil), and drop the pronoun.
Present, future and conditional: nach + eclipsis (nach bhfuil, nach mbeidh).
Regular past: nár + h (nár fhreagair).

lessons.title: An coibhneasta indíreach: a + urú
lessons.en: Where, with whom, whose: a + eclipsis
lessons.rule: When the noun is not the one doing the action (it goes with a preposition such as ann or léi, or with a possessive such as a deartháir), use a and eclipsis, and keep the subject and the preposition: Seo an teach. Tá mé i mo chónaí ann. becomes Seo an teach a bhfuil mé i mo chónaí ann. Bhí becomes a raibh (an bhean a raibh mé ag caint léi) and gheobhaidh becomes a bhfaighidh. A verb beginning with l, m, n, r or s cannot be eclipsed, so it does not change: an cara a rachaidh mé leis.
steps: Keep the whole second sentence, with its subject and ann, léi or leis at the end.
Add a and eclipse the verb: tá becomes a bhfuil, téann becomes a dtéann.
Bhí becomes a raibh, gheobhaidh becomes a bhfaighidh. A vowel takes n-: a n-imrím.

lessons.rule: In the past, a regular verb takes ar and h, and loses d': Sin an siopa ar cheannaigh mé mo bhróga ann. For not, use nár and h: an cailín nár labhair mé léi. steps: Keep the subject, and ann, léi or leis, at the end.

lessons.title: Cé, Cad é agus An té
lessons.en: Who, what and whoever: the direct relative
lessons.rule: Cé (who), Cad é (what) and An té (the one who, whoever) take the direct relative, as in the question words section: a and h, or atá for tá. Cé a d'fhreagair an fón? Cad é a tharla? An té a bhíonn ag caint, ní bhíonn sé ag éisteacht. For not, use nach and eclipsis, or nár and h in the regular past: Cé nach ndearna an obair?
steps: Start with Cé, Cad é or An té.
Add a and put h on the verb, or write atá for tá.
Not: nach + eclipsis, or nár + h in the regular past.

lessons.title: An áit, an fáth, an dóigh
lessons.en: The place where, the reason why, the way that

lessons.title: An t-uatha: an fhréamh
lessons.rule: To tell one person to do something, use the root of the verb on its own, with nothing added: Suigh síos. Druid an doras. Éist. The root is the form a dictionary gives, and every tense is built from it.
steps: Find the verb: an doras a dhruidim.
Use the root on its own: druid, éist, ceannaigh.
Add the rest of the sentence: Druid an doras.

lessons.title: An t-iolra: -aigí agus -igí
lessons.rule: To tell more than one person, add an ending to the root. One-syllable verbs take -aigí after a broad vowel and -igí after a slender one: glanaigí, tógaigí, éistigí, druidigí. Verbs in -aigh or -igh drop it and take -aígí or -ígí: ceannaígí, bailígí. Suigh, nigh and léigh give suígí, nígí and léigí. Verbs that shorten do the same: osclaígí, imrígí. Siúil drops its i and is broad: siúlaigí.
steps: Is the last vowel of the root broad (a, o, u) or slender (i, e)?
Broad: -aigí (glanaigí). Slender: -igí (éistigí).
-aigh or -igh: -aígí or -ígí (ceannaígí, bailígí).

lessons.title: Ná: an t-ordú diúltach
lessons.en: Don't: Ná, and h before a vowel
lessons.rule: To tell someone not to do something, put Ná before the command. Ná does not change a consonant: Ná bris é. Ná druidigí an doras. Before a vowel, Ná adds h: Ná hól é. Ná hith é. Ná héistigí leis.
steps: Write the command: bris, ól, éistigí.
Put Ná in front.
Does the verb begin with a vowel? Add h: Ná hól.

lessons.title: Déanaimis nó Déanadh muid
lessons.rule: For let's, add -aimis to a broad root or -imis to a slender one: déanaimis, fanaimis, cuirimis. Verbs in -aigh or -igh, and verbs that shorten, take -aímis or -ímis: ceannaímis, tosaímis, imrímis. Siúil gives siúlaimis. You will also hear the form with muid: déanadh muid, cuireadh muid, imríodh muid. Both are right. For let's not, put Ná in front: Ná déanaimis.
steps: Take the root: déan.
Add -aimis (broad) or -imis (slender): déanaimis.
Or use -adh or -eadh with muid: déanadh muid.

lessons.title: Na briathra neamhrialta
lessons.rule: Irregular verbs use their root as a command too: Bí, Déan, Ith, Faigh, Abair, Tabhair, Beir, Tar, Téigh. In Ulster, Gabh is often used for go: Gabh abhaile. The plurals are Bígí, Déanaigí, Ithigí, Faighigí, Abraigí, Tugaigí, Beirigí, Tagaigí, Téigí and Gabhaigí. For look, say Amharc; Feic and Cluin are rare as commands (say Éist for listen). Ná works as usual: Ná habair é, Ná tar isteach.
steps: Take the root: tar, abair, tabhair.
More than one person: learn the plural (tagaigí, abraigí, tugaigí).
Not: Ná, with h before a vowel (Ná habair).

lessons.title: Sa seomra ranga
lessons.rule: A teacher usually speaks to the whole class, so most classroom commands are plural: Seasaigí suas. Suígí síos. Osclaígí bhur leabhair. Change do (your, one person) to bhur (your, more than one), and make the noun plural. Bhur eclipses: bhur gcóipleabhair, bhur bpinn.
steps: Make the verb plural: suigh becomes suígí.
Change do to bhur.
Make the noun plural and eclipse it after bhur: do chóipleabhar becomes bhur gcóipleabhair.

lessons.title: Giorrú: -aím agus -ím
lessons.en: Verbs that shorten: I in the present
lessons.rule: Some two-syllable verbs ending in -ail, -ain, -air, -il, -ir or -is squeeze out their last vowel when an ending is added, then take second-conjugation endings: oscail becomes oscl-, so osclaím; imir becomes imr-, so imrím. Add -aím if the short stem is broad, with a, o or u before the last consonants (oscl-, labhr-, codl-), and -ím if it is slender, with i or e (imr-, ins-).
steps: Take the root: oscail, imir, labhair.
Squeeze out the last vowel: oscl-, imr-, labhr-.
Add -aím (broad) or -ím (slender): osclaím, imrím.

lessons.title: An aimsir láithreach: -aíonn agus -íonn
lessons.en: The present: other people, questions and negatives
lessons.rule: With anyone else, add -aíonn or -íonn to the short stem: osclaíonn sí, imríonn siad, insíonn sé, labhraíonn sibh. With muid, write imríonn muid (imrímid is also right). An and Ní work as usual: An imríonn tú peil? Ní labhraíonn sé. A verb beginning with a vowel never changes after An or Ní: Ní osclaíonn an siopa.
steps: Squeeze out the last vowel: oscl-, imr-.
Add -aíonn (broad) or -íonn (slender).

lessons.title: An modh coinníollach: -ódh agus -eodh
lessons.rule: Start from the future, change -óidh to -ódh or -eoidh to -eodh, and add h, or d' before a vowel or f: osclóidh becomes d'osclódh, codlóidh becomes chodlódh, imreoidh becomes d'imreodh. L, n and r take no h: labhróidh becomes labhródh. With mé: d'imreoinn. Muid and siad have two forms: d'imreodh muid or d'imreoimis; d'imreodh siad or d'imreoidís.
steps: Start from the future: imreoidh.
Change -óidh to -ódh or -eoidh to -eodh (-óinn or -eoinn with mé).
Add h, or d' before a vowel or f: d'imreodh, chodlódh.

lessons.title: An aimsir chaite agus an fhréamh: gan ghiorrú
lessons.en: The past and the root: no shortening
lessons.rule: The past uses the root with no ending, so nothing is squeezed out: d'oscail, d'imir, d'inis, labhair, chodail, cheangail, d'fhreagair. Put h on a consonant and d' before a vowel or f, as with any verb. The command to one person is the full root too (Oscail an doras), but the plural command has an ending, so it shortens: Osclaígí, Imrígí, Insígí.
steps: Past: keep the whole root: oscail, imir.
Add h, or d' before a vowel or f: d'oscail, chodail.
An ending is added (osclaígí)? Then squeeze.

lessons.title: Taispeáin, sábháil, úsáid: gan ghiorrú
lessons.rule: Not every two-syllable verb shortens. If the last syllable has a long vowel (a fada), nothing is squeezed out, and the verb takes first-conjugation endings. Taispeáin and sábháil drop the i to become broad: taispeánaim, taispeánann sé, taispeánfaidh, thaispeáin; sábhálaim, sábhálfaidh. Úsáid keeps it: úsáideann, úsáidfidh. Compare oscail, which does shorten: osclaíonn, osclóidh.
steps: Look at the last syllable: is there a fada (áin, áil, áid)?
Fada: do not squeeze. Taispeáin and sábháil drop the i: taispeán-, sábhál-.
Add first-conjugation endings: -aim, -ann, -faidh (slender: -im, -eann, -fidh).

lessons.title: Nigh, suigh, léigh: an aimsir láithreach
lessons.rule: A few short verbs end in -igh but have only one syllable: nigh, suigh, léigh, luigh. They do not take second-conjugation endings. Nigh, suigh and luigh drop -gh and put a fada on the i: ním, níonn sé; suím, suíonn sé; luíonn sé. Léigh drops -igh: léim, léann sé. (Léim also means jump: the sentence tells you which.)
steps: Is the verb one syllable ending in -igh?
Nigh, suigh, luigh: drop -gh (ní-, suí-, luí-). Léigh: drop -igh (lé-).
Add -m for mé, -onn for the others (léigh: -ann).

lessons.title: Nigh, suigh, léigh: caite, fáistineach, coinníollach
lessons.en: One-syllable -igh verbs: past, future and conditional
lessons.rule: The past is the root with h where it can take it: nigh mé, shuigh mé, léigh mé. The future adds -fidh to ní-, suí- and léi-: nífidh, suífidh, léifidh. The conditional adds -feadh with h: nífeadh, shuífeadh, léifeadh (mé: nífinn, shuífinn, léifinn). Muid and siad have two forms: léifeadh siad or léifidís.
steps: Past: the root, with h (shuigh); n and l take no h.
Future: ní-, suí-, léi- + -fidh.
Conditional: h + ní-, suí-, léi- + -feadh (-finn with mé).

lessons.title: An t- roimh ghuta: ainmfhocal firinscneach
lessons.en: Masculine nouns: t- before a vowel
lessons.rule: Irish has no word for a: árasán means flat or a flat. The only article is an (the). A masculine noun that begins with a consonant does not change after an (an bus, an doras), but a masculine noun that begins with a vowel takes t- joined to it with a hyphen: an t-árasán, an t-uisce. Before a capital letter there is no hyphen: an tIúr.
steps: Is the noun masculine? árasán is (it ends in -án).
Does it begin with a vowel? Yes, á.
Put t- in front of it: an t-árasán.

lessons.title: Ainmfhocal baininscneach: an + séimhiú
lessons.rule: After an, a feminine noun that begins with b, c, f, g, m or p takes séimhiú: bean becomes an bhean, fuinneog becomes an fhuinneog. Nouns that begin with d or t never take séimhiú after an, whatever their gender: an deirfiúr, an teilifís. A feminine noun that begins with a vowel does not change: an oíche.
steps: Is the noun feminine? fuinneog is (it ends in -eog).
Does it begin with b, c, f, g, m or p? Yes, f.
Add h after the first letter: an fhuinneog.

lessons.title: An ts: ainmfhocal baininscneach le s
lessons.en: Feminine nouns beginning with s: an ts
lessons.rule: A feminine noun that begins with s followed by a vowel, or by l, n or r, takes t in front after an, with no hyphen: sráid becomes an tsráid, slí becomes an tslí. As the subject or object of a sentence, a masculine noun beginning with s does not change (an siopa, an samhradh), and sc, sm, sp and st never change (an scoil, an spéir). After a preposition and an, though, a masculine s-noun takes t as well: sa tsiopa, sa tSruthán.
steps: Is the noun feminine? sráid is.
Is the s followed by a vowel, l, n or r? Yes, r.
Put t in front of it: an tsráid.

lessons.title: Na + h roimh ghuta
lessons.en: Plural: na, and h before a vowel
lessons.rule: In the plural the article is na for every noun, masculine or feminine. Na leaves a consonant as it is, so the séimhiú of the singular goes (an bhróg, na bróga). Before a vowel na puts h, and the t- of the singular goes: an t-úll becomes na húlla.
steps: Change an to na.
Use the plural: éan becomes éin.
It begins with a vowel, so put h in front: na héin.

lessons.title: Firinscneach nó baininscneach? Na deirí
lessons.rule: Some endings tell you the gender. Feminine: -óg and -eog (fuinneog), -lann (bialann), and -acht or -íocht in a word of more than one syllable (Gaeltacht, filíocht). Masculine: -ín (cailín), -án (cupán), -óir, -eoir and -éir (múinteoir, úinéir), -aire (iascaire) and -adh (geimhreadh). Once you know the gender, you know what an does: an bhialann, an cupán, an t-úinéir.
steps: Look at the ending: bialann ends in -lann.
-lann is feminine.
Feminine with b: add h after an, so an bhialann.

lessons.rule: Put it all together. The prompt tells you the gender (fir. is firinscneach, masculine; bain. is baininscneach, feminine). Masculine: t- before a vowel, no change to a consonant. Feminine: séimhiú on b, c, f, g, m, p; t before s + vowel, l, n or r; no change to d, t, sc, sm, sp, st or a vowel.

lessons.title: An tuiseal gairmeach: ainmneacha buachaillí
lessons.en: Calling a boy or man by name
lessons.rule: When you speak to someone by name, the name is in the vocative case (an tuiseal gairmeach): put a in front and add séimhiú, so Pádraig becomes a Phádraig. A boy's name that ends in a broad consonant also turns slender: add i after the last vowel, so Seán becomes a Sheáin, Ciarán becomes a Chiaráin and Colm becomes a Choilm. Names that begin with a vowel, l, n or r show no séimhiú (a Eoin, a Rónáin).
steps: Put a in front: a Seán.
Add séimhiú: a Sheán.
Seán ends in a broad n, so make it slender: a Sheáin.

lessons.en: Calling people: a chara and a chairde
lessons.rule: Words you call people work like names: a + séimhiú, so múinteoir becomes a mhúinteoir and cara becomes a chara. To speak to a group, use a + séimhiú + the plural: a chairde, a dhaltaí, a pháistí, a chailíní.

lessons.title: An tuiseal tabharthach: réamhfhocal + an
lessons.en: The dative: a noun after a preposition
lessons.rule: A noun after a simple preposition (ag, ar, as, chuig, de, do, faoi, i, le, ó, roimh, thar, trí) is in the dative case (an tuiseal tabharthach), and it keeps its dictionary form. With the article in Ulster, b, c, f, g, m and p take séimhiú: leis an bhus, ón bhanc, faoin chrann. A noun that begins with s followed by a vowel, l, n or r takes t instead, whether it is masculine or feminine: sa tsiopa, ar an tsráid, sa tSruthán. D, t and vowels do not change: ag an doras, ar an tábla. Remember the joined forms: leis an, don, den, faoin, ón and sa.
steps: Join the preposition and an: le + an is leis an.
bus begins with b, so add séimhiú: bhus.
Write it: leis an bhus.

lessons.hint: Preposition + an + b, c, f, g, m, p: add h. s + vowel, l, n or r: ts. D, t and vowels: no change.

lessons.title: An ginideach i ndiaidh an ainm bhriathartha: frásaí coitianta
lessons.en: The genitive after a verbal noun: everyday phrases
lessons.rule: The object of a verbal noun (ag déanamh, ag imirt, ag glanadh) goes into the genitive. With no article, just use the genitive form: ag imirt peile, ag seinm ceoil, ag cur ama amú. With the article, a masculine noun keeps an, takes séimhiú and its genitive ending: ag imirt an chluiche. The t- before a vowel goes (ag ithe an aráin), and d and t do not change (ag ól an tae). A feminine noun takes na, with h before a vowel: ag glanadh na cistine, ag déanamh na hoibre. Learn the common ones as chunks.
steps: Find the object: an obair.
Put it in the genitive: obair is feminine, so na hoibre.
Write it after the verbal noun: ag déanamh na hoibre.

lessons.title: An ginideach i ndiaidh chun, cois, trasna agus timpeall
lessons.en: The genitive after chun, cois, trasna and timpeall
lessons.rule: Four simple prepositions take the genitive, not the dative: chun (to), cois (beside), trasna (across) and timpeall (around). A masculine noun keeps an, takes séimhiú and its genitive ending (timpeall an bhaile, trasna an bhóthair). A feminine noun takes na (trasna na sráide, cois na farraige). D, t and vowels do not take séimhiú: timpeall an tí.
steps: Is the noun masculine or feminine? sráid is feminine.
Feminine: an becomes na.
Give it the genitive ending: sráid becomes sráide, so trasna na sráide.

lessons.title: Má + séimhiú
lessons.rule: Má (if) puts séimhiú on the verb after it: bíonn becomes má bhíonn, feiceann becomes má fheiceann. Tá, deir and verbs that begin with a vowel do not change (má tá, má deir, má itheann). Use the present tense after má even when you mean the future: Má bhíonn sé fliuch amárach, fanfaidh muid istigh. Never put the future tense after má.
steps: Put the verb in the present: bíonn.
Add séimhiú after má: má bhíonn.
The other half can be in the future: fanfaidh muid istigh.

lessons.en: If, in the past: má with the past tense
lessons.rule: Má can also go with the past tense. The verb stays exactly as it is in the past, with its séimhiú or d': má chuaigh sé, má d'ith tú, má fuair sí. Nothing is added and nothing is taken away.
steps: Put the verb in the past: chuaigh.
Write má in front of it and change nothing: má chuaigh.
Finish the sentence: Má chuaigh sé abhaile, cuirfidh mé scairt air.

lessons.title: Dá + urú + an modh coinníollach
lessons.rule: For something imagined or unlikely (if I were, if I had), use dá: put the verb in the conditional and eclipse it (dá mbeadh, dá bhfaighinn, dá n-éistfeá). The other half is in the conditional too, with séimhiú, or d' before a vowel or f (d'fhanfainn): Dá mbeadh airgead agam, rachainn go Meiriceá. R cannot be eclipsed, so after dá, rachainn and rachfá stay as they are: dá rachfá. With muid and siad either form is right: rachadh muid or rachaimis, bheadh siad or bheidís.
steps: Put bí in the conditional and eclipse it: dá mbeadh.
Put the other verb in the conditional with the right person: rachainn.
Write it: Dá mbeadh airgead agam, rachainn go Meiriceá.

example.answer: Dá mbeadh airgead agam, rachainn go Meiriceá.

more.answer: Dá mbeadh airgead againn, rachadh muid go Meiriceá.
more.alt: Dá mbeadh airgead againn, rachaimis go Meiriceá.

lessons.hint: Dá + urú + conditional, and the conditional in the other half.

lessons.title: Mura + urú
lessons.rule: Mura (if not) eclipses the verb after it. Like má, it takes the present when you mean the future (Mura mbíonn tú in am, imeoidh an bus gan thú), and tá becomes mura bhfuil. For something imagined, use the conditional: Mura mbeadh sé ag cur báistí, rachainn amach. In Ulster you will also hear and see muna, which is fine: muna mbíonn.
steps: Put the verb in the present: bíonn.
Eclipse it after mura: mura mbíonn.
Finish the sentence: Mura mbíonn tú in am, imeoidh an bus gan thú.

lessons.title: Má, dá nó mura? Sa Chomhrá
lessons.en: Má, dá or mura? In the speaking test
lessons.rule: In the speaking test, listen to the question and look at the other half of your answer. If it is real or likely, use má + séimhiú and the present (or the past). If it is imagined and the other half is in the conditional, use dá + urú. If you mean if not, use mura + urú. You will often be asked Cad é a dhéanfá dá ...?, and your answer starts with Dá.
steps: Read the other half: thabharfainn is in the conditional.
So the if half is imagined: dá + urú + the conditional.
Answer: Dá mbeinn i mo Phríomh-Aire, thabharfainn ...

example.prompt: Cad é a dhéanfá dá mbeifeá i do Phríomh-Aire? _______ (if: bí, mé) i mo Phríomh-Aire, thabharfainn níos mó airgid do na scoileanna agus do na hospidéil.
example.answer: Cad é a dhéanfá dá mbeifeá i do Phríomh-Aire? Dá mbeinn i mo Phríomh-Aire, thabharfainn níos mó airgid do na scoileanna agus do na hospidéil.

lessons.hint: Real: má. Imagined, with a conditional: dá. If not: mura.

ta-bionn.title: Tá nó bíonn?
ta-bionn.en: Tá or bíonn: now or usually

lessons.title: Bím agus bíonn: an aimsir ghnáthláithreach
lessons.en: Bím and bíonn: what usually happens
lessons.rule: Bí has two present tenses. Tá is for right now; bíonn is for what happens usually, or again and again. For I, the pronoun joins the verb: bím. For we, say bíonn muid (bímid is also right). Everyone else takes bíonn: bíonn tú, bíonn sé, bíonn sí, bíonn sibh, bíonn siad.
steps: Is it a habit? Ar maidin, every morning: yes.
Use bíonn; for mé, join them: bím.
Write it: Bím tuirseach ar maidin.

example.answer: Bím tuirseach ar maidin.

more.answer: Bíonn sé fuar sa gheimhreadh.

lessons.title: Tá nó bíonn?
lessons.en: Tá or bíonn? Now or usually
lessons.rule: Use tá for something true now, at this moment (Tá sé fuar inniu). Use bíonn for a habit, or something that happens again and again (Bíonn sé fuar sa gheimhreadh). Let the time phrase decide: anois, inniu and faoi láthair point to tá; achan lá, go minic, i gcónaí, de ghnáth and ar an Luan point to bíonn.
steps: Find the time phrase: anois.
Anois means right now, so use tá.
Write it: Tá sé ag cur sneachta anois.

example.prompt: (Bí) sé ag cur sneachta anois.
example.answer: Tá sé ag cur sneachta anois.

more.prompt: (Bí) sé ag cur báistí go minic in Éirinn.
more.answer: Bíonn sé ag cur báistí go minic in Éirinn.

lessons.hint: Now: tá. Usually or often: bíonn.

lessons.title: Ní bhíonn agus An mbíonn?
lessons.en: Negatives and questions: Ní bhíonn, An mbíonn?
lessons.rule: For the negative of bíonn, write Ní bhíonn (Ní bhím for I). For a question, write An mbíonn ...? The short answers (freagraí gearra) are Bíonn (yes) and Ní bhíonn (no); to a question with tú, answer Bím or Ní bhím. Compare tá, which becomes Níl and An bhfuil.
steps: Put Ní in front of the verb.
Add séimhiú: Ní bhíonn.
For a question use An and eclipsis instead: An mbíonn?

lessons.title: Bíonn le frásaí ama
lessons.rule: A time phrase that means a habit turns tá into bíonn and níl into ní bhíonn: achan lá, achan Satharn, go minic, i gcónaí, de ghnáth, uaireanta, ó am go ham, sa gheimhreadh, ar an Luan. Riamh (ever) goes with the negative: Ní bhíonn sé in am riamh.
steps: Read the time phrase: sa gheimhreadh.
It is a habit, so tá becomes bíonn.
Add the phrase at the end: Bíonn sé fuar sa gheimhreadh.

lessons.en: Usually, but today: bíonn and tá together
lessons.rule: One sentence can use both: bíonn for the habit and tá for now. Bíonn sé fliuch de ghnáth, ach tá sé grianmhar inniu. This is a good way to add detail to an answer in the speaking test.

lessons.title: Bhíodh: an aimsir ghnáthchaite
lessons.rule: For something that used to happen again and again in the past, use bhíodh, the past of bíonn: Bhíodh sé fuar achan gheimhreadh. For one time in the past, use bhí: Bhí sé fuar inné. For I, say bhínn; for they, bhídís (or bhíodh siad); for we, bhíodh muid (or bhímis). Nuair a bhí mé óg keeps bhí, because it is one stretch of time.
steps: Is it one time or again and again? Achan samhradh: again and again.
So use bhíodh; muid keeps its pronoun: bhíodh muid.
Write it: Bhíodh muid i nDún na nGall achan samhradh nuair a bhí mé óg.

lessons.title: Is é Seán an captaen: ionannas
lessons.en: Saying exactly who: Is é Seán an captaen
lessons.rule: To say exactly who or what someone or something is, when both parts are definite (a name, a noun with an, or a noun with mo, do and so on), use Is + é for a man or a masculine noun, í for a woman or a feminine noun, iad for more than one, then the name, then the definite noun: Is é Seán an captaen. Is í Aoife an duine is sine. Is iad Tomás agus Niamh na captaein.
steps: Both parts are definite: Seán and an captaen.
Seán is a man, so use Is é.
Write it: Is é Seán an captaen.

lessons.title: Aicme nó ionannas?
lessons.rule: Is + noun + é or í says what kind of person or thing someone is: Is dochtúir í Siobhán (Siobhán is a doctor). Is + é or í + name + the definite noun says exactly who: Is í Siobhán an dochtúir (Siobhán is the doctor). If the noun has an, or is followed by a noun with an or na (captaen na foirne), it is definite: use Is é or Is í first.
steps: Is the noun definite? dochtúir has no an: no.
So say what kind: Is + dochtúir + í.
Write it: Is dochtúir í Siobhán.

lessons.title: Is ar maidin a ...: béim a chur ar fhocal
lessons.rule: To stress one part of a sentence, put it first after Is, then a, then the rest: Téim ag rith ar maidin becomes Is ar maidin a théim ag rith (it is in the morning that I go running). The verb after a takes séimhiú (a théim, a chuaigh), a verb with d' keeps it (a d'fhág), a verb that begins with a vowel does not change (a itheann), and tá becomes atá.
steps: Take out the phrase to stress: ar maidin.
Put Is ar maidin first, then a.
Add séimhiú to the verb: a théim ag rith.

lessons.title: Is mise a rinne é
lessons.en: Stressing who: Is mise a rinne é
lessons.rule: To stress who did something, put Is and the emphatic pronoun first (mise, tusa, eisean, ise, muidne, sibhse, iadsan), then a + séimhiú + the verb: Rinne mé é becomes Is mise a rinne é. Tá becomes atá: Is ise atá ag canadh. With a name or a noun, use Is é or Is í: Is é Seán a scóráil an cúl. In the negative, Ní goes on the copula and the verb stays positive: Ní mise a bhris é.
steps: Take out the person to stress: mé.
Put Is mise first, then a.
Keep the verb and drop the old pronoun: Is mise a rinne an cáca.

example.prompt: Béim ar 'mé': Rinne mé an cáca.
example.answer: Is mise a rinne an cáca.

more.prompt: Béim ar 'Seán': Scóráil Seán an cúl.
more.answer: Is é Seán a scóráil an cúl.

lessons.hint: Is mise, tusa, eisean, ise, muidne, sibhse, iadsan + a + séimhiú.
